Impact of Microaeration and the Redox Mediator
Anthraquinone-2,6-Disulfonate on Azo Dye Reduction
and By-Products Degradation
Amanda N. de Barros, Marcos E. R. da Silva, Paulo I. M. Firmino,
Eduardo A. F. de Vasconcelos, and Andre B. dos Santos*
This work assessed the impact of microaeration and the redox mediator
anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonate (AQDS) on both azo dye reduction and
by-products degradation (aromatic amines) in a mesophilic reactor. The
experiment was carried out in an up-flow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB)
reactor with 3.2 L of working volume and hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 24h.
The synthetic effluent contained 50 mg L1 of the dye Reactive Red 2 (RR2). The
reactor was initially operated under anaerobic conditions and, subsequently, was
microaerated with atmospheric air (1 mLmin1) and then supplemented with the
redox mediator (AQDS) at a concentration of 25 μM. The microaeration effect on
dye reduction and by-products formed was not evident. However, AQDS
considerably enhanced RR2 reduction, and its regeneration was not affected by
the presence of oxygen. It seems that the cleavage of the double bond between
nitrogen groups is a much easier way to start the attack of the azo dye, and it is
independent of the presence of oxygen. Thus, the introduction of hydroxyl groups
into the aromatic ring was not playing a role in the color removal process. In
terms of ecological parameters, the ecological niches were maintained, and the
distribution of species increased, despite the majority being generalists, i.e., not
specialized in dye degradation. Furthermore, anaerobic species are dominant over
facultative species, which explains why there was no population diversity recovery
after the microaeration started.
1. Introduction
The textile sector is one of the most representative segments in
industry due to its importance to the economy of developed
countries and because it represents a “ﬂagship” in several
developing countries. In 2015, it was responsible for US$ 291
billion of world exports, in which China, the European Union,
and India remained the top three exporters
of textiles. Altogether, they accounted for
66.4% of world exports.[1] The Brazilian
demand for textile products is still high,
generating wastewater with high amounts
of dyes, organic matter, chemicals, etc.,
which
poses
a
risk
when
discharged
without treatment into surface water. The
difﬁculty to treat efﬁciently colored waste-
water in treatment plants is a constant in
textile industry, as small amounts of dyes
and pigments produce intense coloring.[2]
It is estimated that 109 kg of dyes are
produced every year in the world, among
which 70% are azo dyes (N55N).[3,4]
These dyes are molecules soluble in water,
which can contain one or more ionic
groups, and the most common used are
sulfonic acid and amine groups. These are
considered recalcitrant and non-biodegrad-
able.[5,6] Large amounts of dyes are lost
during industry process and goes to the
environment as wastewater. Efﬂuents con-
taminated with dyes are considered toxic to
aquatic
environment
and
symbiosis
process, and interfere negatively in photo-
synthesis and primary production, because
transparency is reduced.[5]
Some works show that the application of
quinone-based compounds, such as anthraquinone-2-sulfonate
(AQS) and anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonate (AQDS), vitamins,
such as riboﬂavin, or even yeast extract can accelerate electron
transfer and increase color removal.[7,8] Biological azo dye
reduction usually requires anaerobic operation because the
redox condition achieved is more effective for color removal,
whereas removal or biodegradation of the by-products (aromatic
amines) occur commonly in aerobic environment, in which the
products are used as sources of carbon, nitrogen, and energy.[9]
The addition of microaeration, i.e., introduction of low oxygen
concentrations (< 1 L O2 L1 feed),[10] can facilitate the initial
degradation of some aromatic compounds, including BTEX
(benzene, toluene ethylbenzene, and xylenes), hormones, and
pharmaceuticals, because, under microaerobic conditions, some
microorganisms can use oxygen to introduce hydroxyl groups
into the aromatic ring, as in the classical aerobic pathway,
subsequently facilitating cleavage by anaerobic pathway.[11] By

controlling the oxygen levels, the redox potential could be
maintained at the proper levels for dye reduction as well,
therefore, both processes could take place in the same reactor.
Additionally, there is a lack of studies investigating the effect
of redox mediators on dye reduction under microaerobic
conditions, thus accelerating the formation and removal of
by-products under such conditions. Another important point to
investigate is if the microaerobic environment will interfere the
regeneration capacity of the redox mediator, thus affecting
negatively the color removal efﬁciency.
Hence, this work assessed the impact of microaeration and
the redox mediator AQDS on both azo dye reduction and by-
products degradation (aromatic amines) in a mesophilic up-ﬂow
anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactor.
2. Experimental Section
2.1. Reactor
The UASB reactor was made of acrylic plastic and polyvinyl
chloride (PVC) connections for sewage, with a working volume
and hydraulic retention time of 3.2 L and 24 h, respectively. The
inoculum was an anaerobic sludge (30 g of volatile suspended
solids (VSS) per liter), from a mesophilic UASB reactor treating
brewery wastewater. The reactor was completely covered with
aluminum
foil
to
avoid
phototrophic
microorganisms
proliferation.
The inﬂuent was stored at 4 C, and the reactor was operated
at room temperature of 27 C. The biogas produced was
collected and subsequently analyzed by GC (Shimadzu, GC 17A)
according to Firmino et al.[12]
At some stages, a microaeration system was operated to create
an inﬂux of oxygen by pumping atmospheric air into the reactor
through the feeding line at a ﬂow rate of 1 mL min1 (28 C,
1 atm) (Resun Air Pump AC 1000), which corresponds to an
inﬂuent ﬂow rate to air ﬂow rate ratio (Qinf/Qair) of 2.4.
2.2. Synthetic Textile Wastewater
The synthetic wastewater was composed of water, an azo dye, a
carbon source (electron donor), basal medium (nutrients), a
buffer, and a redox mediator (when tested). The dye used in this
research was Reactive Red 2 (RR2) (40% purity, Sigma–Aldrich,
USA) at a concentration of 50 mg L1.
The electron donor (2 g of chemical oxygen demand (COD)
per liter) was ethanol (99.8% purity, Din^amica, Brazil), and the
basal medium composition was prepared according to Firmino
et al.[13] The wastewater was buffered with sodium bicarbonate
(NaHCO3), 1 g NaHCO3/L synthetic inﬂuent to maintain pH
 7. At some stages, AQDS (Sigma–Aldrich) was used as redox
mediator at a concentration of 25 μM. The reagents were used as
purchased, without further puriﬁcation.

This study was carried out in ﬁve stages (Table 1), including the
start-up period (stage I), in which ethanol was the only source of

carbon and energy. During the experiment, there was no change
in the hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 24 h.
Subsequently, after the reactor has reached a steady state, RR2
was introduced at a concentration of 50 mg L1 (stage II). At the
next stage (III), the microaeration started at a ﬂow rate of
1 mL min1 of atmospheric air (Qinf/Qair ratio of 2.4).
At the next stage, the redox mediator AQDS was added at a
concentration of 25 μM (stage IV). Subsequently, the microaera-
tion was turned off at stage V, but the redox mediator was
maintained. The transition between stages was done after
checking dye removal stability (variation up to 10%) in the last
three analysis points (1 week of operation).[12]
After the continuous-ﬂow experiments, a batch assay was
conducted for 10 h, using the same reactor, in order to obtain
kinetic data of dye reduction and aromatic amine removal. Thus,
a peristaltic pump (Watson Marlow, model 323) was used to
recirculate the efﬂuent, 90 rpm, 35 L day1, in order to have a
minimum time outside the reactor.
Along the batch experiment, the feeding pump was turned off,
and the pump used was the Watson Marlow. After sludge
decantation, the supernatant was discarded, and the reactor was
fed with synthetic wastewater. Two batch experiments were
conducted, under anaerobic and microaerobic conditions,
respectively.
2.4. Analyses
The color analysis was performed three times a week, for the
continuous-ﬂow experiment, and every 30 min, for the batch
experiment, by spectrophotometry (Hach, DR  6000). Inﬂuent
samples were previously diluted (1:5) in water, followed by
dilution (1:2)
in a
phosphate
buffer, pH
7 (10.86 g L1
NaH2PO4  2H2O and 5.98 g L1 Na2HPO4  2H2O) and then
centrifuged for 2 min at 13 000 rpm (Eppendorf, Mini Spin). The
efﬂuent samples were ﬁltered and diluted (1:2) in the phosphate
buffer. The absorbance of the dye was read at the wavelength of
513 nm (λmax). Furthermore, a scanning of the samples between
the wavelengths 190 and 700 nm (Hach, DR  6000) was
performed.
COD and total alkalinity (TA) were determined according to
Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewa-
ter,[14] volatile fatty acids (VFA) were determined using the Kapp
titrimetric method and pH was determined by a multiparameter
probe (Hanna, H9828).
At the end of each stage, sludge samples were collected in
order to analyze changes in microbial population dynamics.
Molecular biological analyses were performed as detailed
elsewhere,[12] and bacterial, and archaeal community structure
were evaluated by parameters, such as evenness/functional
organization (Fo), ranged weighted richness (Rr), and Shannon
diversity index (H).[15]
2.5. Statistical Methods
The computer program SigmaStat 4.0 was used for the statistical
data analysis, in which the Mann–Whitney Rank Sum test, a
non-parametric procedure which does not require a speciﬁc data
distribution, was used to compare the performance of the
different stages. The results of the tests were evaluated according
to the p-value. If p  0.05, the null hypothesis is rejected, i.e., the
data groups are considered statistically different.[12]
3. Results and Discussion
3.1. Color Removal under Anaerobic and Microaearobic
Conditions
The efﬁciency of co-substrate removal presented instability at the
initial stages due to the adaptation of inoculum microbiota. After
60 days of operation, the efﬁciency and stability improved
probably due to microbial adaption. At this stage, the COD
removal efﬁciency was 93% (Table 1). pH values were between
6.6 and 7.4, demonstrating good operational performance of the
anaerobic reactor.[16]
After the start-up (stage I), the dye RR2 was introduced at a
concentration of 50 mg L1 (stage II), as shown in Table 1. The
average color removal efﬁciency was 51% (Table 1). Initially,
the removal efﬁciency was approximately 60%, then decreased to
40% and, subsequently, increased to 55% (Figure 1). The highest
efﬁciency at the initial stage occurred probably due to dye
adsorption onto the sludge blanket, which seemed to reach its
saturation point around the day 22 of operation. It is worth
mentioning that the color removal efﬁciency obtained was
considered low, even though the HRT used was high (24 h). The
results are in accordance with Dos Santos et al.,[4] who obtained
an efﬁciency of 56% using an expanded granular sludge bed
(EGSB) reactor and RR2 concentration of 1.25 g L1, although
the HRT used was only 10 h.
On the contrary, Dos Santos et al.[17] report an efﬁciency of
92% and 87% for 0.02 and 0.04 g L1 of RR2, respectively, at a
HRTof 10 h. One possibility for the higher efﬁciency is related to
the low dye concentration used in the experiment, which,
together with a high biomass concentration, promoted a zero
order kinetics and, hence, a high efﬁciency.[17]
During stage III, when microaeration was applied, the system
performance was similar to that at stage II (p ¼ 0.975), whose

microaerobic (stage III) conditions.

color removal was 51% (Figure 1). Thus, under the conditions
tested in the experiment, it was not possible to observe any effect
of microaeration on color removal.
Addition of low oxygen concentration can facilitate the initial
degradation of some compounds.[11] However, it seems that the
cleavage of the double bond between nitrogen groups is a much
easier way to start the attack of the azo dye, and it is independent
of the presence of oxygen. Thus, the azo bond cleavage was not
affected by the presence of oxygen, and the introduction of
hydroxyl groups into the aromatic ring, as in the classical aerobic
pathway, subsequently facilitating cleavage by anaerobic path-
way,[11] was not playing a role in the process. Therefore,
microaeration showed to be an inefﬁcient strategy to speed up
azo dye reduction.
Microaeration would inﬂuence aromatic amines mineraliza-
tion, helping to break the aromatic ring. However, no remarkable
removal was found in the present investigation. Partial or
complete azo dye by-product (aromatic amine) removal by
aerobic processes is reported in the literature.[9] Therefore, the
amount of oxygen must be much higher to increase the oxidation
reduction potential (ORP) of the system, and the aromatic
amines removal would occur by both cell anabolism and
catabolism.
Although the results were unexpected for color and aromatic
amines removal, microaeration would be very important to
remove other compounds present in textile wastewater, such as
adsorbable organic halides (AOX),[18–20] which are recalcitrant
under anaerobic conditions.
The absorption spectrum after RR2 inﬂuent and efﬂuent
scanning during stages II and III is shown in Figure 2.
According to Feng et al.,[21] who worked with reduction and
oxidation of the same azo dye, the absorbance peak at 310 nm are
related to naphthalene ring, whereas the peak at 230 nm are
related to benzene ring. Both structures exist in the dye, and the
divergence between the peaks can be related to groups nearby.
Pinheiro et al.[22] mentioned that absorption peaks at 196, 230,
and 280 nm are possibly related to aniline, one of the aromatic
amines which can be produced from RR2 reduction. Aniline was
indeed detected in an EGSB reactor under thermophilic
conditions, revealing that this compound could not be further
degraded under anaerobic conditions.[21]
Feng et al.[21] showed that, after reductive process, a
signiﬁcant peak at 260 nm appeared, being attributed to the
multi-substituted benzene (e.g., benzene dicarboxylic acid)
produced from degradation of the naphthalene ring. Neverthe-
less, in the present experiment, this peak appeared before dye
reduction. Feng et al.[21] also showed that, when the azo bond is
not
destroyed,
but
hydrogenated
(Ar─NH─NH─Ar’),
an
absorption peak at 245 nm appeared. The absence of this peak
reinforces the hypothesis of azo bond cleavage.
A decrease in the visible region around the absorption peak
(arrow) at 513 nm was found, showing a reduction in dye
concentration (Figure 2). Moreover, RR2 has three absorption
peaks at 230 (peak 1), 260 (peak 2), and around 310 nm (peak 3)
(Figure 2), which are consistent with the results found by Feng
et al.[21] In addition, around 310 nm (peak 3), there was a
decrease in the absorption (Figure 2), indicating that, probably, a
by-product with naphthalene ring in the molecular structure was
removed.
3.2. Color Removal Under Anaerobic and Microaearobic
Conditions with AQDS Addition
The addition of low concentration of AQDS (25 μM) improved
color removal almost immediately, and the average efﬁciency
was 82.5%, around 30% higher compared to stage III (p < 0.001).
This result is similar to Dos Santos et al.,[23] who used an
expanded granular sludge bed (EGSB) reactor (HRT ¼ 10 h) for
RR2 removal and obtained an average efﬁciency of 88%, whereas
an efﬁciency of 56% was obtained when AQDS was absent.
During stage V, without microaeration, the performance was
similar to that of the last stage (p ¼ 0.214), with an efﬁciency of
82% (Table 1, Figure 3). Therefore, the microaeration did not
affect the color removal either in the absence (stages II and III) or
in the presence (stages IV and V) of the redox mediator.
Color removal of azo dyes under anaerobic conditions in the
presence of redox mediator occurs in two steps: the ﬁrst one
consists in an enzymatic reduction of redox mediator by
electrons generated in oxidative processes; and the second one
consists in a chemical transfer of electrons to azo dyes, then
redox mediator is regenerated.[23] Therefore, the results indicate
that the low concentration of oxygen present did not have any

and redox mediator regeneration. The latter ﬁnding is important

compounds present in textile wastewater and AQDS to speed up

not affect negatively the AQDS activity.
The absorption spectrum at stages IV and V showed a higher
decrease in absorbance peak (arrow) at 513 nm (Figure 4)
compared to stages II and III (Figure 2), indicating that a higher
dye reduction was taking place.
In relation to the three peaks present in the UV region
(Figure 4), no signiﬁcant differences between stages IV and V
were found. However, by comparing with stages II and III, a
higher absorbance at peaks 1 and 2 was achieved (Figure 2
and 4), indicating a higher azo dye by-products formation.
Moreover, a higher difference between inﬂuent and efﬂuent
absorbance was observed by analyzing peak 3 (naphthalene ring)
(Figure 2 and 4).
3.3. Color Removal Under Anaerobic and Microaearobic
Conditions with AQDS Addition in a Reactor Operated in
Batch
As the microaeration effect on amines formation and their
subsequent mineralization during the continuous-ﬂow experi-
ment was not clear, a batch test was carried out to analyze
whether the degradation occurred in a different way inside the
reactor. Considering that the HRT of 24 h could be too high, a
hypothesis of formation, and mineralization of amines under
anaerobic and microaerobic conditions was investigated.
Efﬂuent samples were collected every hour, and the total batch
time was 10 h. For anaerobic conditions, results indicate that, at
3 h, there is a peak of a compound with benzene ring (230 nm).
After this time, this peak started to decrease until be equal to
efﬂuent (after 10 h) (Figure 5).
This behavior shows that probably, inside the reactor,
formation and mineralization of compounds, due to dye
degradation, were occurring. The efﬁciency was 73.5% after
10 h, close to the average efﬁciency at stage IV (82.5%). This
indicates that it is possible to work with a lower HRT. Under
anaerobic conditions, after 10 h, it was possible to reach a color
removal close to the one obtained in 24 h (Figure 6).
However, under microaerobic conditions, with the same time,
the efﬁciency was 66.7%, approximately 15% less than that
obtained in 24 h (82%) (Figure 6). This behavior shows that,
probably, due to the establishment of appropriate microaerobic
conditions to remove dyes, this system took more time to reach
the ORP necessary to remove color. In addition, the formation
and reduction of the peaks at both conditions were possible.
3.4. COD Removal and Operational Stability
Operational data for reactors performance are shown in Table 1.
The average efﬂuent pH ranged from 7.2 to 7.9, which is close to
the recommended values.[16] Pearce et al.[24] reported that the
optimum pH for color removal is generally neutral or slightly
alkaline.

anaerobic and microaerobic conditions, with and without AQDS,
as well as its performance in COD removal is shown in Table 1.

The difference between the stages related to COD removal is
statistically different (p < 0.001) for all the stages.
When comparing stages I and II, a slight decrease in COD
removal from 93% to 89% can be observed. The addition of
oxygen by microaeration caused another decrease in COD
removal, from 89% to 86%. The usual slightly positive or
negative effect of microaeration on COD removal will depend on
many factors such as air ﬂow rate, substrate complexity,
microbial community, and others.[25,26]
At stage IV, the redox mediator AQDS was added to the reactor.
Atthis stage,the efﬁciency increasedfrom86%to90%. Adifferent
result was obtained by Firmino et al.,[13] who found almost
identical efﬁciency in a reactor containing AQDS (100 μM).
Cervantes et al.[27] related that the addition of AQDS (30 μM)
increasedthe average CODremovalfrom80%to87%,whenusing
azo acid Orange 7 in a UASB reactor (HRT ¼ 6 h). Albuquerque
et al.[28] aimed to decolorize azo Acid Orange 7 (25mg L1) in the
presence of starch (1150 mgL1) as co-substrate. The authors
observed a decrease in efﬁciency when a redox mediator (50 μM)
was added to an anaerobic–aerobic reactor.
At stage V, the microaeration was turned off, but the AQDS
was maintained in the reactor. At this stage, the COD removal
increased slightly from 90% to 93%, similar to the values found
between stages IV and V, which indicates that the microaeration
promoted a slightly negative impact on organic matter removal.
3.5. Microbial Community
The effect of operational conditions on diversity, evenness, and
richness of the bacterial and archaeal communities was assessed
by unweighted pair group method with arithmetic mean
(UPGMA) clustering analysis based on the Pearson similarity
coefﬁcient.[12] Ecological parameters were obtained according to
Marzorati et al.:[29] range-weighted richness (Rr), Shannon
diversity (H), and functional organization (Fo), for both bacterial
and archaeal communities.
The sludge presented the following parameters: for bacteria,
Rr ¼ 69, H ¼ 2.65, and Fo ¼ 33; whereas, for archaea, Rr ¼ 76,
H ¼ 2.56, and Fo ¼ 40 (Table 2), which indicates that the archaeal
community was dominant in the inoculum.
The results for bacteria show that, after the start-up stage, Rr
was reduced by 20%, H was reduced by 6%, while Fo was
increased by 27%. These parameters indicate that the bacterial
community became slightly more specialized (despite retaining
a medium level specialization) than at the previous stage,
probably because the use of ethanol as substrate. Archaeal
community presented different changes: Rr was increased by
54%, H was increased by 15%, whereas Fo showed no
signiﬁcant change (<5%). These changes indicate that generalist
archaea were favored, increasing the populational parameters,
but maintaining the specialization level at medium range.
At the second stage, the use of azo dye had a positive impact
in both domains: for bacteria, Rr was increased by 154%, and H
was increased by 21%, whereas, for archaea, Rr was increased
by 8%, and H was increased by 6%. Fo for both domains was
reduced by 7%. These results indicate that the introduction of
the dye favored signiﬁcantly the bacterial community and
slightly the archaea. The domains maintained medium levels of
Fo, despite the slight decrease, which indicates that both were
colonized by generalists, thus, no dominant specialized groups
were present.

This result shows that fermentative bacteria are more
important to azo dye reduction than archaea, probably because
archaea cannot directly reduce the dye, as well as due to
competition between methanogenesis and azo dye reduction for
equivalents available.[31]
At stage III, microaeration started, promoting different level
of impacts for each domain: for bacteria, Rr was decreased by
12%, H and Fo showed no signiﬁcant change (<5%); for archaea,
Rr was decreased by 42%, H was decreased by 8%, and Fo was
decreased by 8%. These results indicate that the number of
bacterial and archaeal species decreased signiﬁcantly, despite
their distribution presented little to no changes.
Even though there was a quantitative decrease of bacterial and
archaea species, there was no signiﬁcant change in dye removal
because the required quantity of electrons for color removal was
too low.[32]
At stage IV, the addition of AQDS under microaerobic
conditions promoted further impacts than those observed at the
previous stage: for bacteria, Rr was decreased by 75%, H was
decreased by 6%, and Fo was decreased by 10%; for archaea, Rr
was decreased by 42%, H showed no signiﬁcant change (<5%),
and Fo was decreased by 14%. The signiﬁcant impacts observed
for both domains on Rr, despite the slight changes in H and Fo,
once again indicate that the carrying capacity was reduced, thus
reducing the number of species, but not their distribution.
Considering that, after the microaeration, Rr was decreased at
both stages (III and IV), it can be inferred that the anaerobic species
were probably the dominant over the facultative species, since no
populationalrecoverywasobservedaftertheintroductionofoxygen.
Although there was a huge impact on the microbial
community, the dye removal efﬁciency increased, indicating
that the capacity of electron transfer of the system was improved
by the addition of the redox mediator AQDS.
At stage V, the reactor returned to anaerobic condition, thus
promoting a new impact in both domains: the results for bacteria
showed that the anaerobic condition promoted increase in
populational parameters, as Rr was increased by 236%, H
showed no signiﬁcant change (<5%), whereas Fo was decreased
by 83%. The results for archaea revealed a completely different
outcome, as Rr and H showed no signiﬁcant change (<5%),
whereas Fo was increased by 20%. The number of species
increased drastically, which indicates that the carrying capacity
for
bacteria increased.

maintaining

decreasing Fo indicate that the ecological niches were main-
tained, and the distribution of species increased, despite the
majority being generalists, thus not specialized in dye degrada-
tion. This conﬁrms that reduction of the azo bond is not an
inherent property of methanogens.[32]
4. Conclusions
Considering the conditions applied to the present experiment, it
was not possible to show any microaeration effect on dye
reduction and by-products formed.
Low concentration of oxygen did not have any negative effect
on both dye reduction and redox mediator regeneration. Because
of that, AQDS considerably enhanced RR2 reduction.
It seems that the cleavage of the double bond between
nitrogen groups is a much easier way to start the attack of the azo
dye, and it is independent of the presence of oxygen. Thus, the
introduction of hydroxyl groups into the aromatic ring was not
playing a role in the process of color removal. However,
microaeration
would
be
important
to
textile
wastewater
treatment, in which other recalcitrant compounds under
anaerobic conditions would be present.
In terms of ecological parameters, the ecological niches were
maintained, and the distribution of species increased, despite
the majority being generalists, thus not specialized in dye
degradation. Furthermore, anaerobic species are dominant over
facultative species, which explains why there was no population
diversity recovery after the microaeration started.
